Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events

Memory.value: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning

Negative Appraisals.value: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it

vignette: Samira sat in the worn velvet armchair, her hands folded tightly in her lap, her gaze fixed on the double doors of the tutoring room. At seventy-seven, she was single, living quietly in a sunlit apartment that doubled as her classroom. She had come to believe she was a weak person, a conviction that settled into her bones long ago, though she never voiced it aloud. Her work as a tutor anchored her days, but it also became the specific setting where her symptoms unfolded with quiet precision. During her lessons, she always positioned her chair within arm’s reach of the exit. It was not a conscious decision so much as a settled habit; when the doorbell rang or a car backfired down the street, she felt the familiar tightening in her chest and shifted closer to the threshold. She avoided television programmes and films that showed cities under siege or soldiers marching, and she turned the newspaper over when headlines mentioned conflict zones. Watching such material made her throat constrict, as though the screens were broadcasting directly into her living room. What frightened her most was not the noise itself, but the way her mind would drag her back. The traumatic event had occurred over four decades ago, when she was a young civilian navigating a Middle Eastern city caught in heavy bombardment. She had been grading papers in a ground-floor classroom when the first shells struck. The air pressure shifted, the wooden frames of the windows shuddered, and a fine grey dust began to fall from the plaster ceiling like snow. Samira remembered the exact moment the terror rose: not as a distant record, but as a physical weight pressing against her ribs. She felt the same sharp, breathless panic that she had experienced in that room, as though the ceiling were collapsing again. When she closed her eyes now, she could still see the dust motes dancing in the lamplight and hear the distant rattle of artillery. Something as ordinary as a student dropping a textbook on the hardwood floor could instantly bring the full memory forward without warning. She would sit very still, her breath catching, certain that the floor was giving way, that the room was tilting. What happened next was not a gradual remembering but a sudden immersion; the classroom walls seemed to thin, and she felt as though the bombardment were happening right then. In the years since, she had developed a quiet routine of avoidance. She told herself that if she let herself think about those weeks, the emotions would spill over and she would not be able to handle them. So she kept her thoughts carefully compartmentalized, focusing on lesson plans and schedules rather than the past. Yet she often caught herself dwelling on how she used to be before the event—how she had once laughed easily, traveled without checking the sky, and moved through crowds without scanning for threats. She compared her younger self to her present condition, noting how much lighter life had felt then. At the same time, a deep emotional numbness had settled over her. She went through the motions of teaching and preparing tea, but she felt dead inside, as though a layer of glass separated her from the world. The numbness did not feel like peace; it felt like stillness, like holding her breath. Now, at seventy-seven, Samira had finally come to seek help. The tipping point had arrived on an ordinary Tuesday when a student’s father called to report a nearby airshow, and the distant roar of jets rolled through her open window. In that moment, she sat rigid, certain that the sound was not a rehearsal but a return. She realized that her chair by the door, her guarded television habits, and her careful steering away from news broadcasts were no longer just preferences; they were boundaries she was maintaining to keep the past at bay. What she feared most was not another war, but the possibility that her own mind would betray her, that she would unravel if she let the memories rise unchecked. What she hoped for was simply to sit in a room without counting the exits, to watch a film without turning away, and to remember the bombardment as something that happened to her, rather than something that was still happening to her. She hoped, above all, to stop feeling so entirely cut off, and to trust that she could bear the weight of her own life again.
